newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: PLDT '96 net higher than expected - analysts.
newsitem.headline: PLDT '96 net higher than expected - analysts.

text.p: Philippine Long Distance Telephone Co (PLDT), the country's biggest telephone company, posted higher-than-expected net income for 1996 on Wednesday and analysts said the firm was set to extend those gains this year.
PLDT posted 1996 net income of 6.44 billion pesos, up 11.98 percent from 5.751 billion pesos the previous year.
A Reuters poll of five brokerages last month predicted an average 1996 net profit of 5.22 billion pesos.
"It was a bit of a surprise. The increase was brought about by call volumes and manpower reduction," said Jonas Ferrer, research director at Pryce Securities.

"The results are slightly above expectation... PLDT is transforming itself into a more balanced revenue-based company with less dependence on international calls. It has started the ball rolling in that direction," Louie Hilado, an analyst with ING Barings, said.
PLDT said its local network revenues rose by 25.8 percent to 7.95 billion pesos ($302.28 million) from 6.322 billion pesos.
The growth came from an increase in the number of telephone lines to 1.518 million from 1.196 million in 1995.
Revenues from national long distance calls, which make up 15.6 percent of operating revenues, surged by 27.7 percent in 1996.
But growth in international revenues was less dramatic, by 5.2 percent at 15.867 billion pesos from 15.085 billion in 1995. International revenues make up 55.4 percent of operating revenues.
The company said operating expenses rose only 2.4 percent to 17.246 billion pesos because of lower expenses and an employee redundancy programme.
Analysts said that apart from increasing call volumes and lower expenses, PLDT would also benefit from a proposed adjustment in tariffs.
Due to stiffer competition and pressure from inter-connecting foreign telephone companies, PLDT has sought to cut international toll rates and raise basic phone charges.
Subscribers are now charged a fixed monthly subscription under which they are entitled to an unlimited number of local calls as the exchanges do not have a metering system.
U.S. telephone companies have been pressing for a steep cut in international tariffs in a bid to generate more calls.

At present, the rate between the United States and the Philippines is $1 per minute and U.S. firms have sought to cut that to 38 cents. Calls to the United States comprise the bulk of PLDT's international call revenues.
PLDT's application for the tariff adjustments is before the National Telecommunications Commission.
"If the proposal for rate rebalancing pushes through, then PLDT can weather the threat of accounting rate reduction this year," said Ricardo Puig, analyst at Peregrine Securities.
Accounting rate refers to the sharing of revenues from international phone calls between inter-connecting phone firms.
"Tariff re-balancing, if approved, will compensate for the decreasing accounting rates," Alexis Cabel, analyst at AngPing Securities said.
